data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms as a methodological rule grounded in the asymmetry of risk, not as an inductive inference about future probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly stated that choosing a theory for action requires an inductive belief in its future success.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference for corroborated theories cannot be distinguished from assigning them higher subjective probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'asymmetry of risk' argument implicitly assumes that the future will resemble the past (uniformity of nature).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which remains unproven) and the rational decision to act upon it. Choosing the best-tested theory is a pragmatic wager based on the fact that while no amount of testing proves a theory true, a single severe test can falsify it. Therefore, the well-corroborated theory has survived risks that eliminated its competitors; preferring it minimizes the risk of acting on a known falsehood without claiming it is probably true. This relies on the 'asymmetry of risk' where rejecting a robust theory exposes the agent to easily refuted alternatives, whereas accepting it exposes the agent only to potential future falsification which has not yet occurred.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
